assumptions: Leak onset is inferred from the shape of the heap curve, not from any event: the investigation variously placed the start at 23:47 and at 23:51. Neither is corroborated by a log line or change record.

That no deploy, release, config or feature-flag change occurred is assumed from empty query results across an eight-day window and an empty flag-provider history. An unrecorded or out-of-band change remains possible and could not be excluded from the evidence available.

The recurring 'account page request failed - UpstreamTimeout: payment authorization timed out' errors and the 0-2% per-minute error-rate warnings are treated as pre-existing background noise, because they appear at the same rate from 22:46 onward, well before any heap growth. They were not investigated further.

Recovery was judged from a single observation that the service was at baseline about twenty seconds after the restart. No soak period was observed, and no check was made that the heap was not simply starting the same climb again from zero.

The restart is a symptomatic mitigation. No heap dump, allocation profile or object-retention evidence was collected, so the specific leaking code path is unknown and the leak should be assumed still present in the running build.
The draft pull request proposed by the code-fix agent was not reviewed, tested or confirmed to address the actual leak; it is an unverified suggestion.

The recorded incident duration (0.44 hours) does not match the alert and mitigation timestamps, which are about one minute apart. The discrepancy was not reconciled; user-visible degradation plausibly began around 23:47, well before the alert fired.
The reported error-rate impact is negative, i.e. the measurement does not indicate any additional failed traffic. Customer impact is therefore characterised as latency-only.
input.executive_summary: Shortly after midnight UTC on 20 September, the storefront service that renders customer account pages began consuming memory steadily without releasing it. As memory filled up the service spent more and more time on garbage collection, and pages became noticeably slower to load — roughly three times slower at the tail by the time the alert fired. Customers were not locked out: requests kept succeeding at their usual rate, and the small trickle of payment-authorization timeouts visible in the logs was present for at least an hour and a half beforehand and is unrelated to this event. The automated on-call system picked up the alert, reviewed the preceding hour and a half of metrics and logs, found no deployment or configuration change anywhere in the previous week that could explain it, and concluded the service was leaking memory. It restarted the affected process about forty seconds after the alert, and confirmed within a minute that memory and response times were back to normal. A draft code change intended to address the leak has been opened for engineers to review. The restart relieves the symptom but does not fix the leak, so the same slow build-up should be expected to recur until the underlying code is corrected.
input.root_cause: io-shop leaked heap memory: from roughly 23:47 on 19 Sep the process heap climbed monotonically from its ~466MB baseline to ~1.42GB against a 2GB limit with no intervening restart (process_start_time_seconds was constant) and no deploy, release or config change recorded in the preceding eight days, so the growth came from an allocation path in the already-running build rather than from a change. Rising GC pressure dragged p95 latency from ~217ms to ~743ms, which is what tripped the HighMemoryUsage alert; the underlying allocation site was never identified, only the symptom was cleared by restarting the process.
